stem: A 48-year-old man presents with fever, drooling, muffled voice, and painful swelling beneath the jaw after a recent lower molar tooth infection. Examination shows bilateral submandibular swelling, elevation of the tongue, and tenderness of the floor of the mouth. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
stemHtml: A 48-year-old man presents with fever, drooling, muffled voice, and painful swelling beneath the jaw after a recent lower molar tooth infection. Examination shows bilateral submandibular swelling, elevation of the tongue, and tenderness of the floor of the mouth. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? (Question Id: 506048)
keywords: Fever + drooling + muffled voice → Suggests upper airway compromise from deep neck infection
Bilateral submandibular swelling + tongue elevation → Classic sign of submandibular space infection
Recent lower molar infection → Odontogenic source spreading to deep neck space
Painful floor of mouth + induration → Indicates cellulitis of sublingual/submandibular spaces
keywordsHtml:
1. Fever + drooling + muffled voice → Suggests upper airway compromise from deep neck infection
  2. Bilateral submandibular swelling + tongue elevation → Classic sign of submandibular space infection
  3. Recent lower molar infection → Odontogenic source spreading to deep neck space
  4. Painful floor of mouth + induration → Indicates cellulitis of sublingual/submandibular spaces

B.title: Ludwig angina
B.body: This is a rapidly progressive, life-threatening cellulitis of the submandibular, sublingual, and submental spaces. It classically arises from lower molar infections and causes elevation of the tongue due to sublingual space involvement. Airway obstruction is the major risk and requires emergency management. The presentation with drooling, muffled voice, and bilateral submandibular swelling is highly characteristic.
B.bodyHtml: This is a rapidly progressive, life-threatening cellulitis of the submandibular, sublingual, and submental spaces. It classically arises from lower molar infections and causes elevation of the tongue due to sublingual space involvement. Airway obstruction is the major risk and requires emergency management. The presentation with drooling, muffled voice, and bilateral submandibular swelling is highly characteristic.
B.clinicalReasoning:
Odontogenic infection spreads to submandibular spaces
Causes “woody” induration of floor of mouth
Leads to posterior tongue displacement → airway compromise
Requires emergency airway protection + IV antibiotics
System: Head & Neck / Oral Cavity / Upper Airway
B.clinicalReasoningHtml:
• Odontogenic infection spreads to submandibular spaces
  • Causes “woody” induration of floor of mouth

A.title: Acute necrotizing ulcerative gingivitis
A.body: A severe ulcerative gum infection typically associated with pain, bleeding gums, halitosis, and punched-out interdental papillae. It is linked to poor oral hygiene and immunosuppression. It does not cause deep neck space swelling or airway compromise. Clinical features are localized to gingiva rather than submandibular spaces.

C.title: Oral candidiasis
C.body: Fungal infection caused by Candida species, commonly seen in immunocompromised patients or after antibiotics. It presents with white curd-like plaques that can be scraped off. It is superficial and does not involve deep neck spaces or cause systemic airway symptoms.

  • Not associated with dental abscess spread

D.title: Primary herpetic gingivostomatitis
D.body: Acute HSV-1 infection causing painful oral ulcers, fever, and gingival inflammation. It usually affects children or young adults and presents with diffuse oral vesicles and ulcers. It is self-limited and does not cause deep neck swelling or airway obstruction.

E.title: Tuberculous oral ulcer
E.body: A chronic, painless or mildly painful ulcer due to Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection. It is rare and usually associated with pulmonary or systemic TB. It presents as a persistent ulcer rather than acute swelling or airway symptoms.

keyConcept: This question tests recognition of deep neck space infection originating from odontogenic source, specifically Ludwig angina. Key diagnostic clues are submandibular swelling, floor of mouth induration, tongue elevation, and airway symptoms (drooling, muffled voice), which indicate an emergency airway-threatening condition requiring immediate intervention.

diagram.description: This diagram illustrates the pathogenesis, anatomical spread, clinical features, airway compromise, and management principles of Ludwig angina. It demonstrates how infection from a lower molar tooth spreads into the submandibular, sublingual, and submental spaces, leading to tongue elevation and potential airway obstruction. Key emergency signs such as drooling, muffled voice, bilateral submandibular swelling, and respiratory distress are highlighted along with the importance of early airway management and intravenous antibiotic therapy.
